screens.title: Advanced Material Techniques & Optimizations
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will connect practical optimization techniques with creative shader design. You will learn why material instancing matters for draw calls and how Shader Graph empowers artists to build custom visual effects without writing low-level shader code. We’ll start with the performance payoff: sharing the exact same material across many objects can allow Unity to batch and reduce draw calls, and creating material instances lets you vary appearance without multiplying assets. Then we’ll open Shader Graph ideas — nodes, connections, and properties — and show how these elements let you make effects like a simple outline or vertex-based wind. Finally, we’ll cover texture practices: right-sizing textures, using compression, and packing textures into atlases to reduce G P U memory and texture swaps. A short hands-on activity will guide you through creating a vertex-offset outline shader and exposing properties so artists can tweak values in the Inspector. By the end you’ll understand when to rely on the Standard Shader, when to craft a custom shader, and how small texture and material choices can scale to big G P U savings. Consider how these methods could change performance on your current scene.

screens.title: Material Instancing — Definition & impact
screens.narratorSegment: Material Instancing is a pattern where multiple objects share a base material while allowing per-object property variation without creating new material assets for each object. The key performance idea is simple: Unity can batch draw calls for objects that use the exact same material and shader. If you duplicate materials for small color changes, Unity treats each duplicated asset as a separate material and often emits additional draw calls. A Material Instance lets you vary properties via a property block or G P U instancing so that objects still refer to the same underlying material structure. A concrete example: imagine many rocks using a base M_Rock material. If half the rocks need a slightly different tint, creating dozens of separate material assets would increase draw calls. Instead, use a material instance or enable G P U instancing and vary the Albedo color via a property at runtime. Common misconception: some learners assume changing any per-object property prevents batching; the truth is batching depends on whether the shader, render state, and material identity remain compatible. Always validate using Unity’s frame debugger. Takeaway: reuse the same material asset when possible and use instances or property blocks to introduce variation without multiplying draw calls. How might you restructure your scene to share materials more aggressively?

keyIdea.title: Material Instancing in one line
keyIdea.text: Share the same material asset and vary properties with instances to preserve batching and reduce draw calls.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Material Instancing
What is a Material Instance?
A variation of a base material that keeps the same shader and structure but exposes property differences so Unity can still batch rendering when possible.
Definition: Multiple objects reference a shared material or shader while per-object values are supplied via property blocks or instanced parameters.
Why it matters: Reduces draw calls and GPU overhead in scenes with many repeated assets like foliage or modular pieces.
Common mistake: Duplicating materials for small color changes, which increases draw calls unnecessarily.
Concrete example
Use one base material M_Rock and vary Albedo with a material property block or GPU instancing rather than creating M_Rock_Variant1, M_Rock_Variant2, etc.
Visual checklist
  • Same shader and render state across objects
  • Identical material identity where possible
  • Use property blocks for per-instance tweaks
Key Takeaway

Use shared materials and instances to keep draw calls low; profile results with the frame debugger.

screens.title: GPU Instancing vs Material Instancing
screens.narratorSegment: Often the terms 'G P U instancing' and 'material instancing' are used together, but they describe related and distinct behaviors. G P U instancing is a rendering technique where the same mesh and material are drawn many times with different per-instance data passed to the G P U, allowing a single draw call to render multiple objects. Material instancing, in the chapter's usage, emphasizes sharing material assets and varying properties without creating separate material assets per object. They overlap: G P U instancing requires compatible shaders and often benefits from shared materials, while material instancing makes it easier to vary appearance without producing unique material assets that prevent batching. Concrete example: a field of identical grass blades can use G P U instancing to draw many blades with a single draw call while passing per-instance offsets for sway. If you instead create slightly different materials per patch, you may lose G P U instancing benefits. A common misconception is believing G P U instancing automatically applies to any material change; in practice the shader must support instanced properties and the render state must match. Practical rule: design shaders and materials with instancing in mind—use instanced properties for per-object data, keep render states uniform, and avoid duplicating materials when variation can be encoded per-instance. Will your shader expose instanced properties for the variations you need?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › GPU vs Material Instancing
Side-by-side
GPU Instancing
Single draw call for many identical meshes; uses per-instance data for transforms and small parameters.
Material Instancing
Share material assets and vary properties through property blocks or exposed parameters to preserve batching.
Example:
A field of identical grass: use GPU instancing with per-instance sway. If you create many unique materials for color variation, you remove the benefit of GPU instancing.
Checklist to enable instancing
  • Shader must support instanced properties.
  • Render states (blend, culling) must match across instances.
  • Avoid unique material assets for each variation when possible.
Pro tip

Prefer passing color or small offsets as instanced properties rather than duplicating materials. Use property blocks for per-object tweaks when instancing is not enabled.

screens.title: Shader Graph Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Shader Graph breaks shader creation into visual building blocks. Nodes perform operations or supply data — for example Sample Texture 2D reads a texture, Multiply scales values, and Fresnel produces edge intensity. Connections are the lines that move data from node outputs to inputs, defining the computation flow that will compile to shader code. Properties are the exposed variables you define in the graph so that a material using the shader shows color pickers, texture slots, or numeric sliders in the Inspector. A concrete example: create a Color property named OutlineColor and a Float property named OutlineWidth; the color feeds the base color in the fragment stage while the float scales vertex offsets in the vertex stage. A common misconception is that Shader Graph is only for simple effects; in reality it can produce complex, optimized shaders comparable to hand-written code. However, each node adds cost, so designers should profile performance and remove unnecessary math. The practical architecture is: Properties at the top drive nodes, nodes compute per-vertex and per-fragment values, and the Master/Fragment outputs write final color and surface data. As a reflective question: which visual parameter in your project would be most useful to expose as a property so artists can iterate quickly?

Nodes, Connections, Properties
Nodes perform math or texture lookups, connections define flow, and properties expose values to artists.
Sample Texture 2D
Reads color data from a texture property.
Multiply / Add
Basic arithmetic used to blend, scale, or offset values.
Position & Normal
Used for vertex manipulation or lighting calculations.
Property examples
- Color: OutlineColor
- Float: OutlineWidth (default 0.01)
- Texture2D: MainTex
Misconception

Not every node is free. Complex node trees add GPU cost. Remove operations that are not visually necessary.

screens.title: Build the Outline Shader (Step-by-step)
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through a practical Shader Graph build for a simple outline using vertex offset and an exposed color. Start by creating a Lit or Unlit Shader Graph and add the following properties: a Float named OutlineWidth defaulting to 0.01, and a Color named OutlineColor. Add a Position node set to Object space and a Normal Vector node also in Object space. Multiply the Normal Vector by the OutlineWidth float — this yields a vertex offset along normals. Add the result to Position with an Add node and connect it to the Vertex Position output so geometry is pushed outward. For color, connect OutlineColor to the Base Color (or Fragment color) so the outline draws as that color. Important setting: in Graph Settings set Render Face to Both (or Front And Back) so the offset shows as a silhouette. A concrete example you can test: a sphere with OutlineWidth 0.02 and a saturated color will clearly show the effect. A common mistake is pushing positions too far, which causes silhouette artifacts; keep offsets small and test with different meshes. Finally, save the graph, create a Material, and tweak the exposed parameters in the Inspector to iterate quickly. How would you adapt the graph to produce a height-based gradient instead of a single outline color?

keyIdea.title: Build summary
keyIdea.text: Use Position + Normal × OutlineWidth for vertex offset and expose OutlineColor and OutlineWidth as properties for artist control.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Outline Shader Walkthrough
Step-by-step
Create properties and connect Position and Normal to push vertices away along normals.
// Graph steps (informational)
1. Create Float property: OutlineWidth = 0.01
2. Create Color property: OutlineColor
3. Add Position node (Object space)
4. Add Normal Vector node (Object space)
5. Multiply: Normal * OutlineWidth
6. Add: Position + (Normal*OutlineWidth)
7. Connect Add -> Vertex Position
8. Connect OutlineColor -> Base Color / Fragment
9. Graph Settings: Render Face = Both; Surface = Opaque
Test case
Sphere: OutlineWidth 0.02, OutlineColor bright magenta.
Common error
Too-large offsets cause silhouette overlap and Z-fighting; keep values conservative.
Material creation
Save the Shader Graph, then create a Material from the graph asset. Adjust OutlineWidth and OutlineColor from the Inspector to iterate quickly.
Check your understanding

Why does setting Render Face to Both make the outline visible? Consider how vertex offsets affect backfaces.

screens.title: Expose Properties & Artist Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Exposing properties in Shader Graph converts a static shader into an artist-friendly tool. Properties appear as Inspector controls on materials, enabling color pickers, sliders, and texture slots without opening the graph. For our outline shader, exposing OutlineWidth and OutlineColor lets artists iterate quickly across multiple objects. A concrete workflow: author the graph with properly named properties, save, then create a material and assign it to objects. Artists adjust OutlineWidth in the material Inspector and can test different values across scenes. A misconception is that every parameter should be exposed; instead, expose only those artists need to tune, keeping the graph compact and performant. Another practical tip: use descriptive property names and sensible defaults so artists understand the expected range. If you need per-object uniqueness while maintaining batching, expose instanced properties and enable G P U instancing in the material. Finally, document which properties are safe to animate or change at runtime and which should remain static to preserve batching. As a reflective question: which two parameters would you expose first for your shader to maximize artist freedom without harming performance?

Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Expose Properties
Expose parameters for artists
Properties convert graph inputs into Inspector controls. Name and default values matter.
Example properties
OutlineWidth (Float, default 0.01), OutlineColor (Color), MainTex (Texture2D)
Enable GPU instancing
If per-object data is required, mark properties as instanced and enable GPU instancing on the material.
Workflow card

  2. Save graph and create a Material
  3. Adjust property from Material Inspector

Exposing many parameters is not always better. Limit exposure to what artists will actually use and profile the shader when adding features.

screens.title: Texture Optimization: Size, Compression, Atlases
screens.narratorSegment: Textures are often the largest VRAM consumers in a build. Optimization starts by choosing an appropriate max size: detail on distant objects can use smaller textures without a visible quality loss. Unity’s texture import settings let you set a Max Size and a Compression format (for example block compression formats appropriate to the target platform). Compression reduces memory at the cost of small visual artifacts, but those artifacts are often acceptable and far better than uncompressed assets that bloat builds. A texture atlas combines many small textures into one larger texture to reduce the number of texture bindings the G P U must perform, which improves batching and lowers draw call overhead. Concrete example: packing multiple UI sprites into a single atlas reduces texture swaps when rendering a composite HUD. Common mistake: keeping high-resolution 4K textures for tiny decals or distant props; instead, scale down such textures and rely on tiling or detail maps where appropriate. Always test compressed builds on target hardware to validate visual fidelity and memory savings. Final takeaway: right-size, compress, and atlas textures where it gives a clear performance win, and measure the impact rather than guessing.

keyIdea.text: Right-size textures, use platform-appropriate compression, and pack small textures into atlases to reduce memory and draw call cost.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Texture Optimization
Key texture strategies
Max size, compression, and atlasing are primary levers to reduce VRAM and binding overhead.
Max Size: Reduce resolution for distant or small objects; use tiled textures for repeating surfaces.
Compression: Choose formats like ETC2 or ASTC depending on platform to shrink memory use.
Atlas: Pack many small textures into one texture to reduce swaps and improve batching.
Concrete example
UI sprites: one atlas instead of many PNGs reduces texture bindings and memory overhead. Test the compressed build to verify visual trade-offs.
Common mistake

Using uncompressed PNG textures everywhere increases build size and VRAM dramatically. Use Unity compression for deployed builds.

screens.title: Profile and Simplify Shaders
screens.narratorSegment: When you author a custom shader, you are responsible for its cost. Profiling is essential: use Unity’s Frame Debugger and Profiler to see shader cost per draw and which shader passes are expensive. A practical process is: build the required visual effect, then simplify the graph by removing or combining nodes that contribute little to the final look. For example, replace multiple Multiply and Add chains with a single blend when mathematically possible. Another tactic is to use shader variants to support low and high quality paths; expose toggles or define keywords so you can compile a cheaper shader for mobile and a richer one for PC. A concrete example: a complex noise-based distortion can be replaced at low quality with a simple panner texture to emulate motion. A common misconception is assuming visual parity is required across all platforms; instead create quality tiers. Finally, test shader performance with many instances of the object in a scene, because costs scale with instance count. Takeaway: profile early, simplify aggressively, and offer shader variants for different hardware targets. Profile and Simplify Shaders means measure shader cost, simplify unnecessary math, and provide quality variants to support diverse hardware without sacrificing visuals where it matters.. In practical terms, keep shader graph efficient for your target hardware. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Profile, then simplify

Simplification tactics:

Concrete example
Replace a costly procedural noise for low-end builds with a simple panner texture and a lower sample rate, keeping the high-end procedural version for stronger hardware.

Optimizing shaders often yields larger performance gains than small mesh or texture tweaks; profile to find the biggest wins.

screens.title: When to Choose Custom Shaders
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between the Standard Shader and a custom shader is an important design decision. Start by asking: does the Standard Shader support the look you need? If you require PBR accuracy, complex metalness or roughness workflows, the Standard Shader is usually best. Choose a custom shader when you need non-PBR aesthetics like toon shading, or when you require per-vertex manipulations such as wind or vertex-based distortions. Another deciding factor is performance: custom shaders let you remove unused PBR calculations and craft cheaper lighting models when appropriate. A concrete example: foliage that needs procedural sway cannot be achieved by the Standard Shader alone; vertex position manipulation via Shader Graph is the correct choice. A common misconception is that custom shaders always cost more; properly written shaders can be simpler and faster than the fully featured Standard Shader for specialized use. Decision hierarchy: prefer Standard Shader for general PBR needs, use Shader Graph for stylized or procedural effects, and profile the custom shader against the Standard Shader to confirm the trade-offs. Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › When to use Custom Shaders
Decision steps
  1. Do you need a non-PBR look? If yes, consider custom shaders.
  2. Do you need vertex manipulation or time-based procedural motion? Use Shader Graph.
  3. Can the required effect be approximated with maps or the Standard Shader? If so, prefer built-in shaders.
Examples
Use Standard Shader
Photorealistic metal, wood, and PBR surfaces where built-in lighting models suffice.
Use Custom Shader
Toon shading, outline effects, vertex wind, time-based distortions, and special transparency behaviors.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls & Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Before you finish, keep a short list of practices to avoid common pitfalls. First, avoid duplicating materials for tiny visual changes; it multiplies assets and draw calls. Second, avoid leaving high-resolution textures on small or distant objects; right-size and compress instead. Third, don’t add expensive node chains in Shader Graph unless the visual gain justifies the cost; always profile. Fourth, document which shader properties are safe to animate at runtime and which may block batching. A practical habit is to maintain a lightweight test scene that stresses your most common asset types — many small props, foliage, or repeated modular pieces — and use this scene for profiling whenever you change shaders or textures. Another habit is to set sensible defaults for exposed properties so that materials look acceptable without tweaking. A common misconception is assuming visual quality always demands heavier assets; often a carefully tuned cheaper shader and compressed textures deliver a similar perceived quality with much better performance. Final takeaway: make profiling and documentation part of your shader workflow so you can iterate artistically while staying within performance budgets.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will connect practical optimization techniques with creative shader design. You will learn why material instancing matters for draw calls and how Shader Graph empowers artists to build custom visual effects without writing low-level shader code. We’ll start with the performance payoff: sharing the exact same material across many objects can allow Unity to batch and reduce draw calls, and creating material instances lets you vary appearance without multiplying assets. Then we’ll open Shader Graph ideas — nodes, connections, and properties — and show how these elements let you make effects like a simple outline or vertex-based wind. Finally, we’ll cover texture practices: right-sizing textures, using compression, and packing textures into atlases to reduce G P U memory and texture swaps. A short hands-on activity will guide you through creating a vertex-offset outline shader and exposing properties so artists can tweak values in the Inspector. By the end you’ll understand when to rely on the Standard Shader, when to craft a custom shader, and how small texture and material choices can scale to big G P U savings. Consider how these methods could change performance on your current scene.

By the end of this chapter you will understand both practical optimization techniques and creative shader construction. First, you will learn Material Instancing: why sharing the same material and varying properties correctly leads to fewer draw calls, and how that improves performance in scenes with many repeated objects. Second, you will be introduced to Shader Graph: its nodes, connections, and properties, and how to expose parameters to the Inspector so artists can tweak values without touching the graph. Third, you’ll identify when a custom shader is appropriate versus the Standard Shader, including examples such as stylized outlines, vertex-based wind on foliage, or time-based portal distortion. Fourth, you will apply basic material and texture optimizations—choosing correct texture max sizes, enabling compression formats suitable for your target platform, and using texture atlases to reduce texture swaps. Each objective pairs a hands-on skill with why it matters: performance, artistic control, or memory savings. These abilities will help you make scenes that look better while running faster on target hardware.

This second objectives slide clarifies the skills you will actively demonstrate. You will set up material instances and observe how identical materials allow Unity to batch draw calls, then make controlled property changes that keep the underlying material structure shared. You will author a simple outline effect in Shader Graph by combining Position, Normal, Multiply and Add nodes, and you will expose an OutlineWidth float and an OutlineColor property to the material Inspector so artists can tweak results without opening the graph. You will identify at least two reasons to choose a custom shader over the Standard Shader, such as stylized rendering or vertex manipulation for procedural motion. Finally, you will apply optimization checks: measure texture max size, choose a compression format and create a small texture atlas where practical. These are not abstract goals — they are hands-on checkpoints you can verify in your project to show improved batching, controllable shader properties, and reduced texture memory usage.

Material Instancing is a pattern where multiple objects share a base material while allowing per-object property variation without creating new material assets for each object. The key performance idea is simple: Unity can batch draw calls for objects that use the exact same material and shader. If you duplicate materials for small color changes, Unity treats each duplicated asset as a separate material and often emits additional draw calls. A Material Instance lets you vary properties via a property block or G P U instancing so that objects still refer to the same underlying material structure. A concrete example: imagine many rocks using a base M_Rock material. If half the rocks need a slightly different tint, creating dozens of separate material assets would increase draw calls. Instead, use a material instance or enable G P U instancing and vary the Albedo color via a property at runtime. Common misconception: some learners assume changing any per-object property prevents batching; the truth is batching depends on whether the shader, render state, and material identity remain compatible. Always validate using Unity’s frame debugger. Takeaway: reuse the same material asset when possible and use instances or property blocks to introduce variation without multiplying draw calls. How might you restructure your scene to share materials more aggressively?

Often the terms 'G P U instancing' and 'material instancing' are used together, but they describe related and distinct behaviors. G P U instancing is a rendering technique where the same mesh and material are drawn many times with different per-instance data passed to the G P U, allowing a single draw call to render multiple objects. Material instancing, in the chapter's usage, emphasizes sharing material assets and varying properties without creating separate material assets per object. They overlap: G P U instancing requires compatible shaders and often benefits from shared materials, while material instancing makes it easier to vary appearance without producing unique material assets that prevent batching. Concrete example: a field of identical grass blades can use G P U instancing to draw many blades with a single draw call while passing per-instance offsets for sway. If you instead create slightly different materials per patch, you may lose G P U instancing benefits. A common misconception is believing G P U instancing automatically applies to any material change; in practice the shader must support instanced properties and the render state must match. Practical rule: design shaders and materials with instancing in mind—use instanced properties for per-object data, keep render states uniform, and avoid duplicating materials when variation can be encoded per-instance. Will your shader expose instanced properties for the variations you need?

Shader Graph breaks shader creation into visual building blocks. Nodes perform operations or supply data — for example Sample Texture 2D reads a texture, Multiply scales values, and Fresnel produces edge intensity. Connections are the lines that move data from node outputs to inputs, defining the computation flow that will compile to shader code. Properties are the exposed variables you define in the graph so that a material using the shader shows color pickers, texture slots, or numeric sliders in the Inspector. A concrete example: create a Color property named OutlineColor and a Float property named OutlineWidth; the color feeds the base color in the fragment stage while the float scales vertex offsets in the vertex stage. A common misconception is that Shader Graph is only for simple effects; in reality it can produce complex, optimized shaders comparable to hand-written code. However, each node adds cost, so designers should profile performance and remove unnecessary math. The practical architecture is: Properties at the top drive nodes, nodes compute per-vertex and per-fragment values, and the Master/Fragment outputs write final color and surface data. As a reflective question: which visual parameter in your project would be most useful to expose as a property so artists can iterate quickly?

We'll walk through a practical Shader Graph build for a simple outline using vertex offset and an exposed color. Start by creating a Lit or Unlit Shader Graph and add the following properties: a Float named OutlineWidth defaulting to 0.01, and a Color named OutlineColor. Add a Position node set to Object space and a Normal Vector node also in Object space. Multiply the Normal Vector by the OutlineWidth float — this yields a vertex offset along normals. Add the result to Position with an Add node and connect it to the Vertex Position output so geometry is pushed outward. For color, connect OutlineColor to the Base Color (or Fragment color) so the outline draws as that color. Important setting: in Graph Settings set Render Face to Both (or Front And Back) so the offset shows as a silhouette. A concrete example you can test: a sphere with OutlineWidth 0.02 and a saturated color will clearly show the effect. A common mistake is pushing positions too far, which causes silhouette artifacts; keep offsets small and test with different meshes. Finally, save the graph, create a Material, and tweak the exposed parameters in the Inspector to iterate quickly. How would you adapt the graph to produce a height-based gradient instead of a single outline color?

Exposing properties in Shader Graph converts a static shader into an artist-friendly tool. Properties appear as Inspector controls on materials, enabling color pickers, sliders, and texture slots without opening the graph. For our outline shader, exposing OutlineWidth and OutlineColor lets artists iterate quickly across multiple objects. A concrete workflow: author the graph with properly named properties, save, then create a material and assign it to objects. Artists adjust OutlineWidth in the material Inspector and can test different values across scenes. A misconception is that every parameter should be exposed; instead, expose only those artists need to tune, keeping the graph compact and performant. Another practical tip: use descriptive property names and sensible defaults so artists understand the expected range. If you need per-object uniqueness while maintaining batching, expose instanced properties and enable G P U instancing in the material. Finally, document which properties are safe to animate or change at runtime and which should remain static to preserve batching. As a reflective question: which two parameters would you expose first for your shader to maximize artist freedom without harming performance?

Textures are often the largest VRAM consumers in a build. Optimization starts by choosing an appropriate max size: detail on distant objects can use smaller textures without a visible quality loss. Unity’s texture import settings let you set a Max Size and a Compression format (for example block compression formats appropriate to the target platform). Compression reduces memory at the cost of small visual artifacts, but those artifacts are often acceptable and far better than uncompressed assets that bloat builds. A texture atlas combines many small textures into one larger texture to reduce the number of texture bindings the G P U must perform, which improves batching and lowers draw call overhead. Concrete example: packing multiple UI sprites into a single atlas reduces texture swaps when rendering a composite HUD. Common mistake: keeping high-resolution 4K textures for tiny decals or distant props; instead, scale down such textures and rely on tiling or detail maps where appropriate. Always test compressed builds on target hardware to validate visual fidelity and memory savings. Final takeaway: right-size, compress, and atlas textures where it gives a clear performance win, and measure the impact rather than guessing.

When you author a custom shader, you are responsible for its cost. Profiling is essential: use Unity’s Frame Debugger and Profiler to see shader cost per draw and which shader passes are expensive. A practical process is: build the required visual effect, then simplify the graph by removing or combining nodes that contribute little to the final look. For example, replace multiple Multiply and Add chains with a single blend when mathematically possible. Another tactic is to use shader variants to support low and high quality paths; expose toggles or define keywords so you can compile a cheaper shader for mobile and a richer one for PC. A concrete example: a complex noise-based distortion can be replaced at low quality with a simple panner texture to emulate motion. A common misconception is assuming visual parity is required across all platforms; instead create quality tiers. Finally, test shader performance with many instances of the object in a scene, because costs scale with instance count. Takeaway: profile early, simplify aggressively, and offer shader variants for different hardware targets.
